title: Below the Line
passages:
The Marrow groaned as the wave caught her beam-on, rail burying until green water washed the deck. Sol didn't wait for the roll-back. She was already moving, one hand on the shrouds, the other snatching the coiled heaving-line from the pinrail where it lived for exactly this. Nia beat her to the boat-hook, aluminum shaft warm from the sun they'd had at noon, and didn't ask what to do — just ran the hook out over the stanchion, braced her boots on the wet nonskid, and waited for the next wallow to bring the water up to them.

"There — starboard quarter, twenty meters!" Wren's voice cracked over the deck speaker, thin with cold and the wind stealing words. She stood frozen at the winch, slate dark in her hand, the drum silent behind her.

Sol didn't look up. "Got him. Nia, hook the collar. I'll take the line."

The boat-hook dipped, caught, missed, caught again on the second roll — the orange webbing of Dey's harness, torn loose from its tether. Nia's arms locked, shoulders hiked to her ears, hauling dead weight through water that didn't want to give him up. Sol took the line two-handed, walking it back hand-over-hand, boots sliding on the deck's cant. The Marrow heaved the other way, rail lifting, and the water rushed off like a flushed tank, leaving Dey dangling in the hook's grip, half-in half-out, a seal pup caught in a net.

"Steady!" Sol barked, and Nia planted herself, muscles jumping under her soaked jacket.

They swung him inboard together on the next roll, a graceless tangle of limbs and rope, and dropped him on the nonskid like a sack of wet cement. Dey didn't gasp. Didn't cough. His lips were the gray of old ash, eyes open but fixed on nothing, pupils blown wide against the dim. Water bubbled at the corner of his mouth, thin and slow. His chest moved — barely — a reflex the deep hadn't finished killing yet.

"Dey." Sol dropped beside him, fingers finding carotid, wrist, the soft place under the jaw. Pulse thready, skin cold as the bilge. "Dey, look at me."

His eyes didn't shift. Didn't blink. The storm screamed in the rigging and the Marrow took another hit, but the man on the deck didn't flinch, didn't shrink, didn't do anything a living body should do when the world tries to shake it apart.

Nia crouched on his other side, face pale in the running lights, one hand hovering over his chest like she wanted to press down and couldn't decide where. "He's heavy," she said, quiet. "Too heavy. Like the water's still in him."

Sol's jaw tightened. She peeled back Dey's eyelid with a thumb, watched the pupil stay round and dead. "The deep doesn't let go easy. Wren — get the slate. Now."

Wren didn't move. The winch drum sat silent behind her, the slack line coiling in the scuppers like a dead snake. Her slate glowed faint in her hand, the same eleven seconds she'd found in her own record blinking steady at the top of the build.

"Wren!" Sol's voice cracked the wind. "The slate. His slate. Read it."
